solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Corrupt policeman you imprisoned in anger (6)

indicatorNotes.imprisoned in: MP and U are locked up inside the word for anger

blocks.note: U = you, as in text messages

annotation.surface: A bent officer holds someone in a fit of rage.
annotation.walkthrough: "Corrupt" reads as the policeman's failing, but it is the definition, used as an adjective. IRE holds MP + U to give I-MPU-RE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both words describe something morally tainted or debased.

entries.clue: Sponge off Mark? Ace idea! (7,4)

indicatorNotes.off: off = gone bad or wrong, so the letters go astray

annotation.surface: Someone cheers the plan of scrounging from a man called Mark.
annotation.walkthrough: "Sponge off" looks like a phrase meaning to scrounge; split it, and "Sponge" is the definition while "off" works on the letters. Madeira cake is a plain British sponge cake.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this firm, plain loaf-shaped cake is one kind of sponge.

entries.clue: Habitual criminal a usurping revolutionary detains (5)

indicatorNotes.detains: the phrase holds the answer inside it
indicatorNotes.revolutionary: turning round, so the held letters read backwards

blocks.note: the letters spanning crimina(L A USU)rping

annotation.surface: A repeat offender joins a coup and takes someone prisoner.
annotation.walkthrough: The criminal and the usurper both sound like people to be defined, but they are only the letters that hold the answer, read right to left.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what is habitual is what normally happens.

entries.clue: European crook insane to lift flipping books (8)

indicatorNotes.crook: crook = bent or out of order, so the letters are rearranged
indicatorNotes.to lift: to lift = to pick up and carry, so the shuffled letters take in the books
indicatorNotes.flipping: the books are turned over, so OT reads TO

blocks.note: INSANE rearranged, then opened up after ES
OT = Old Testament, a set of books; flipped to TO

annotation.surface: A mad European crook steals some books in a fit of madness.
annotation.walkthrough: "European crook" reads as a person, but "European" is the definition and "crook" works on INSANE. The rearranged INSANE takes in TO: ES-TO-NIAN.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: someone from the Baltic state on the Gulf of Finland is one kind of European.

entries.clue: A dope case for constabulary bureau (6)

indicatorNotes.case for: a case is the outside, so only the outer letters of constabulary are used

blocks.note: the dope and the gen are both slang for inside information

annotation.surface: A drug case that goes to the police department.
annotation.walkthrough: "Dope" and "case" set up a drugs bust, but dope here is information, and "case" asks for the outside of the next word.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both are offices that provide a service, like a travel bureau.

entries.clue: A Republican involved in trial settled (2,4)

indicatorNotes.involved in: R becomes part of the inside of the word for trial

annotation.surface: A Republican is caught up in a court case that has now been resolved.
annotation.walkthrough: A + T(R)EST. The trial in the surface is a court case; in the wordplay it is a test.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: something settled, like sediment or a quarrel, is still and no longer moving.

entries.clue: Tearful English gangster accepts proposal (9)

indicatorNotes.accepts: E + AL takes MOTION in between

blocks.note: Al Capone, the crossword's usual gangster
a motion is a proposal put to a meeting

annotation.surface: An English hoodlum agrees to a proposal, maybe of marriage, and weeps.
annotation.walkthrough: E and AL together hold MOTION: E-MOTION-AL.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: someone close to crying is overcome by feeling.

entries.clue: Prison of fire (3)

blocks.note: to sack someone from a job, also American slang

annotation.surface: A jail built of, or consumed by, flames.
annotation.walkthrough: "Fire" reads as a noun, but it is the verb, to sack someone.
annotation.definitionFit: Both senses are American slang: the one is a jail, the other a verb for dismissing a worker.

entries.clue: Something edgy? Avoiding jury, perhaps (8,5)

blocks.note: a jury is one kind of panel or board

annotation.surface: A nervous defendant tries to get out of facing a jury.
annotation.walkthrough: "Edgy" suggests nerves, but a skirting board runs along the edge of a room where the wall meets the floor, so the definition is a playful one.
annotation.definitionFit: A cryptic sense: the strip of wood along the foot of a wall sits at the edge of the floor.

entries.clue: Dead wig thief or speeder? (4-5)

blocks.note: a rug is slang for a wig

annotation.surface: A list of crooks: someone who steals hairpieces, or someone driving too fast.
annotation.walkthrough: "Speeder" suggests a fast driver; here it is someone on speed, the amphetamine, and the question mark flags the pun.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a user of speed, the amphetamine, is one kind of user of narcotics.

entries.clue: Northern yob catches pig’s outburst (4)

indicatorNotes.catches: OIK catches N and holds it inside

blocks.note: an oik is British slang for a loutish youth

annotation.surface: A northern lout grabs a pig as it squeals.
annotation.walkthrough: OI(N)K. "Pig" is also slang for a police officer, which suits the puzzle's crime theme, but here it is the farm animal.
annotation.definitionFit: A descriptive definition: the grunt a pig lets out, written as a word.

entries.clue: Inside, gang’s head rubbed out deputy, say (4-2)

indicatorNotes.rubbed out: rubbed out = erased, so the G goes

blocks.note: the filling is the inside of a sandwich or pie
the first letter of gang, removed from the end of FILLING

annotation.surface: Someone in the gang kills the leader's second in command.
annotation.walkthrough: "Inside" looks like the prison sense, but it is a noun: the filling. "Rubbed out" is gangland slang for murdered, used here to erase a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by "say": a deputy stands in for someone else.

entries.clue: Most gruff agents punched informer (8)

indicatorNotes.punched: SPIES punch a hole in RAT and sit inside it

annotation.surface: The grumpiest secret agents beat up the snitch.
annotation.walkthrough: RA(SPIES)T. "Most gruff" reads as describing the agents, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a voice at its harshest and hoarsest.

entries.clue: Model pinches type of car model for excitement (11)

indicatorNotes.pinches: to pinch is to steal, so SIMULATION takes T into itself

blocks.note: a simulation is a model of something
the Model T, Ford's famous car

annotation.surface: A model steals a car to get a thrill.
annotation.walkthrough: S(T)IMULATION. The first "Model" is a model of something, not a fashion model; the second belongs to the Model T.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean being roused or stirred up.

entries.clue: Port a grand perjurer opens around one (8)

indicatorNotes.opens: C comes first, at the opening

annotation.surface: A liar in court is circling a big sum of money.
annotation.walkthrough: "Port" might be wine; here it is a harbour city. Cagliari is the capital of Sardinia.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Sardinian capital is a seaport on the island's south coast.

entries.clue: Recoil as trite swindler displays unction (4,5)

indicatorNotes.displays: the phrase shows the answer inside itself

blocks.note: the run starts at the end of recoil and stops after the first letter of swindler

annotation.surface: People back away from a con man whose charm is too smooth and stale.
annotation.walkthrough: In the surface, unction means a greasy, flattering manner. As the definition it means the Catholic rite of anointing the dying, known as extreme unction.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: extreme unction, anointing the dying, is one of the sacraments given at the end of life.

entries.clue: One with nothing to hide in nick (4)

indicatorNotes.to hide: NIL hides A by wrapping around it

annotation.surface: An innocent suspect held in a police cell.
annotation.walkthrough: N(A)IL. "Nick" is British slang for both a police station and to arrest; the surface uses the station and the definition the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang synonyms: both verbs mean to catch or arrest a criminal.

entries.clue: Husband police trap in a small town (8)

indicatorNotes.in: in = placed inside, so STING sits within A and S

blocks.note: a sting is an undercover operation to catch criminals

annotation.surface: A husband is caught in a police set-up in some little town.
annotation.walkthrough: H + A(STING)S. "Small town" wants to be the definition, but "small" only gives the S. Hastings is a seaside town in East Sussex.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the East Sussex seaside resort, famous for the battle of 1066, is a town.

entries.clue: Off-shore banks which a bad criminal mastermind’s behind? (4)

annotation.definition2: which a bad criminal mastermind’s behind?

blocks.note: ridges of sand lying off the shore

blocks.clueFragment: which a bad criminal mastermind’s behind?
blocks.note: a failed crime boss ends up in jail; the question mark flags the playful reading

annotation.surface: A crime boss who hides money in offshore banks.
annotation.walkthrough: "Off-shore banks" suggests tax havens; here they are sandbanks. The second half is cryptic: a bad mastermind gets caught and ends up behind bars.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: sandbanks across a river mouth or off a coast, and the iron rods of a prison cell.

entries.clue: Aim to get hooligan in trouble yourself (2,3,3)

annotation.surface: Advice: try to get a thug into trouble on your own.
annotation.walkthrough: "In trouble" reads as one phrase, but it splits: "in" joins the two pieces, and "trouble yourself" is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to put in maximum effort is to really exert, or trouble, yourself.

entries.clue: Ultimate of felons breaks marriage agreement (6)

indicatorNotes.Ultimate of: the ultimate is the last, so the last letter of felons
indicatorNotes.breaks: to break into something is to force a way inside, so S forces its way into UNION

annotation.surface: The worst of the criminals wrecks a couple's wedding pact.
annotation.walkthrough: UNI(S)ON. "Marriage agreement" looks like a single phrase; "agreement" alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: acting together in harmony, as voices singing the same note.

entries.clue: Criticise a rotten criminal I put inside (4,4)

indicatorNotes.criminal: criminal = wrong, so the letters are jumbled
indicatorNotes.put inside: I goes into the jumbled letters

annotation.surface: Someone attacks a crook they themselves put in jail.
annotation.walkthrough: "Rotten criminal" reads as a pair, but "rotten" is fodder and "criminal" the instruction. TEAR(I)NTO.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to rip into someone verbally is to criticise them fiercely.

entries.clue: Chief of police rubbish, Spooner said (3,3)

indicatorNotes.Spooner said: the Rev Spooner swapped the first sounds of words

blocks.note: a cop is a police officer; it takes the T sound from the next word
tat is British for cheap rubbish; it takes the C sound from the word before

annotation.surface: The head of police talks nonsense, according to Spooner.
annotation.walkthrough: "Chief of police" reads as one title; only "Chief" is the definition. Tat is British for cheap, shoddy goods.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal idiom for whoever is in charge, the boss.

entries.clue: Chap who did lines bobby finally nicked (5)

blocks.note: old British slang for a policeman, like bobby named after Sir Robert Peel, founder of the Met; the final letter is dropped

annotation.surface: A man who snorted cocaine is caught at last by the police.
annotation.walkthrough: "Did lines" suggests drugs; it means wrote verse. George Peele was an Elizabethan poet and playwright.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Elizabethan poet and dramatist wrote lines of verse.

entries.clue: American coppers’ round (4)

blocks.note: a qualifying round of a race or contest

annotation.surface: An American police patrol.
annotation.walkthrough: "Round" reads as a patrol beat; it is a round of a competition.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: US slang for the police, and a preliminary round in sport.

entries.clue: In hearing, I will give judgement (3)

indicatorNotes.In hearing: in the hearing of a listener, so by sound

blocks.note: the pronoun, said aloud, matches the organ of sight

annotation.surface: A judge announces a ruling at a court hearing.
annotation.walkthrough: "Hearing" sounds like a court session, which suits the theme, but it tells you to go by sound.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiomatic sense: having a good eye for something means judging it well.

entries.clue: Plain and clear cops good with this on occasion (9)

indicatorNotes.cops: to cop is to catch, so SERENE catches G
indicatorNotes.on occasion: only some letters of this turn up: every other one

annotation.surface: A simple observation: the police are fine with this now and then.
annotation.walkthrough: "Plain" looks like a partner for "clear"; it is the definition, a grassy plain. SEREN(G)E + TI.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the vast grassland of Tanzania and Kenya is a famous plain.

entries.clue: Capital offence lacks primary motive (6)

indicatorNotes.lacks primary: the primary, or first, letter is missing

blocks.note: betraying the state was a crime punishable by death; the first letter T goes

annotation.surface: A crime that could hang you, committed without a real motive.
annotation.walkthrough: A capital offence is one that once carried the death penalty; "capital" has nothing to do with cities or big letters here.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the grounds or cause for doing something.

entries.clue: Noticing drugs in half-finished jail (6)

indicatorNotes.in: the drugs go inside the jail

blocks.note: Sing Sing, the New York prison, cut in half

annotation.surface: Spotting narcotics being smuggled into a half-built prison.
annotation.walkthrough: S(EE)ING. Sing Sing is a famous maximum-security prison in New York State.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both mean taking in something with the eyes.
